chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim from Safwan ibn Yahya from Hammad ibn Isa and Ibn Abi Umayr from Umar ibn Udhaynah from Zurarah ibn A'yan, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the one who performs al-Mufrad (individual) Hajj during the surplus time, and he said: 'Al-Mut'ah.' I said: 'What is Al-Mut'ah?' He said: 'He enters into Hajj in the months of Hajj; when he circumambulates the House and prays two rak'ahs behind the Maqam, and runs between Safa and Marwah, he shortens (his prayers) and becomes Muhsir (free from Ihram restrictions); when it is the Day of Tarwiyah, he enters into Hajj, performs the rituals, and upon him is the Hady (sacrificial animal).' I said: 'What is the Hady?' He said: 'Its best is a camel, its middle is a cow, and its lowest is a sheep.' And he said: 'I have seen the sheep adorned with a thread or a cord.'

key_terms.أَحَلَّ: To exit the state of Ihram restrictions after completing Umrah rituals.
key_terms.الْمُتْعَةُ: Combined Hajj (Hajj al-Tamattu'), where the pilgrim performs Umrah first, exits Ihram, and then enters Ihram for Hajj.
key_terms.الْمُفْرِدَ: Individual Hajj, where the pilgrim performs Umrah and Hajj separately or together without exiting Ihram.
key_terms.الْهَدْيُ: The sacrificial animal required for Mut'ah and Qiran Hajj.
key_terms.بَدَنَةٌ: A mature camel, considered the best type of Hady.
key_terms.تُقَلَّدُ: Adorned or decorated, specifically with a cord around the neck.
key_terms.قَصَّرَ: To shorten the four-rak'ah prayer to two rak'ahs, a ruling for travelers.
key_terms.يَوْمُ التَّرْوِيَةِ: The 8th of Dhu al-Hijjah, when pilgrims proceed to Mina.
key_terms.يُهِلُّ: To enter the state of Ihram by reciting the Talbiyah.

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between Mufrad and Mut'ah Hajj and what are the ritual requirements for each?
ai.summary: This hadith from the Tahdhib clarifies the procedural mechanics of Hajj al-Tamattu', where the pilgrim performs Umrah first and then assumes Ihram for Hajj on the 8th of Dhu al-Hijjah, distinguishing it from Hajj al-Mufrad. It specifies the obligatory sacrificial animal (Hady) with a clear hierarchy of preference—camel, cow, or sheep—reflecting the scholarly emphasis on the pilgrim's financial capacity. The mention of marking the animals with thread or silk underscores the practical ritual details preserved in Shia fiqh.
